contributions.headingText: Ectopic meningioma is a meningothelial neoplasm occurring entirely outside intracranial and intraspinal cavities. Meningothelial hamartoma represents a developmental rest, composed of non-neoplastic arachnoid cells. In both, a CNS connection must be excluded.
2A01.0Z & XH11P5 Meningeal tumours, unspecified & Ectopic meningioma

Acceptable: extradural meningioma; extracranial/extraspinal meningioma; extraneuraxial meningioma; heterotopic meningioma; cutaneous meningioma; calvarial meningioma; intraosseous meningioma; meningothelial choristoma; rudimentary meningocoele; sequestrated meningocoele; meningothelial rest; meningothelial heterotopia.

More than 90% of ectopic meningiomas occur in the head and neck region. Orbital examples have no dural connection. Other locations include the skull, sinonasal tract, oropharynx, lung, mediastinum, middle ear, scalp, parotid gland, and neck. Meningothelial hamartomas most commonly occur as solitary scalp masses, usually in the occiput. Rare multiple meningothelial hamartomas or familial forms have been reported {8496446}. Rests have also been described in the lung (meningothelial-like nodules) and lymph nodes, among other sites {29939782; 28315423}.

The presenting signs and symptoms of ectopic meningiomas vary greatly, with the most common pattern being that of a painless, slow-growing mass. Meningothelial hamartoma is typically detected as an incidental scalp mass or dimple, sometimes with alopecia and/or tenderness. It may be associated with underlying or distant skeletal anomalies or congenital melanocytic naevus {22420725}.

Ectopic meningiomas are rare. In one review, they accounted for 1.6% of all resected meningiomas and arose at all ages, with bimodal peaks in the second decade and in the fifth to seventh decades of life {11117866}. There was a slight female predominance. Meningothelial hamartomas are typically found in neonates or infants, with no known sex or racial predisposition {21906138}.

Four histogenetic hypotheses have been postulated for ectopic meningiomas: meningothelial cells carried along nerve sheaths exiting the skull or vertebral column, ectopic arachnoid cells, meningothelial cells displaced during trauma, and pluripotent mesenchymal cells capable of undergoing meningothelial differentiation or metaplasia. Meningothelial hamartomas in the scalp are considered pathogenetically related to meningocoeles and meningoencephalocoeles, but without an intracranial connection. In other locations, they are often incidental, possibly representing ectopic rests or metaplastic meningothelial-like cells (e.g. pulmonary nodules).
Molecular studies are lacking, but one intranodal rest in a patient with Cowden syndrome indirectly implicated the PTEN gene {28315423}.

Ectopic meningiomas are similar to their CNS counterparts but are more invasive. Colour and consistency vary with cellularity, collagen deposition, and tumour grade, but a rubbery tan-white mass is most common. Calvarial meningiomas are typically hyperostotic {24997535}. Hamartomas are solitary nodules; plaques; or spongy tan-grey, red, or flesh-coloured lesions in cutaneous and/or subcutaneous scalp.

The same range of histological appearances and grades encountered intracranially may be seen in ectopic meningiomas, with benign meningothelial tumours being most common. In the scalp, hamartomas usually show slit-like spaces resembling lymphatics. However, they are lined by meningothelial (rather than endothelial) cells. Well-formed meningothelial clusters and psammoma bodies can also be encountered. Highly sensitive and specific immunohistochemical markers are generally lacking, with coexpression of vimentin, EMA, and progesterone used most consistently {10800982}. A newer marker, SSTR2A {26195322}, can be expressed in pulmonary meningothelial-like nodules {29939782}. Because meningiomas may express p63, this marker does not reliably distinguish epithelial neoplasms {23924346}. Ultrastructurally, they contain overlapping cytoplasmic processes resembling interlocking pieces of a jigsaw puzzle, as well as desmosomes and other intercellular junctions.
The cytological features of ectopic meningothelial lesions resemble those of their CNS counterparts.
Essential: a meningothelial rest or neoplasm located entirely outside of, and with no connection to, the CNS.

As with other meningiomas, tumour grade and extent of resection play important prognostic roles. Intraosseous skull-base cases have higher recurrence rates than those of the convexity. Distant metastases have been reported in about 6% of cases, mostly in anaplastic (malignant) examples {11117866}. Hamartomas are usually cured by surgery alone, with only rare recurrences.
